To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) mutations on both alleles in DNAH5 were found in 15% (13/89) of a non-pre-selected cohort of patients with PCD; (ii) DNAH5 mutations are not restricted to a specific phenotype; (iii) the ultrastructural defects are heterogeneous; (iv) DNAH11 and DNAI1 genes are rarely mutated in PCD
mutations in DNAH5 are found in 15% non-preselected PCD patients.
DNAH5 is the major gene responsible for primary ciliary dysgenesis, but other genes remain to be identified.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of mutations in PCD patients and with a better understanding of the molecular bases of the disease.
the molecular characterisation of the PCD phenotype and the genetic heterogeneity of this condition.
the identification of mutations in the PCD gene DNAH5 in a non-selected cohort of patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PCD is a genetically heterogeneous disease and that DNAH5 accounts for only 15–20% of a non-selected cohort of patients.
PCD is a genetically heterogeneous disorder and that the genetic diagnosis of PCD is still incomplete.
mutations of DNAH5 are responsible for only 15-20% of the PCD cases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic basis of PCD is still not completely understood and that the clinical diagnosis remains challenging.
mutations in DNAH5 are responsible for 15% of PCD patients.
the genetic heterogeneity of PCD is not restricted to DNAH5, and that the identification of mutations in this gene is only the first step in the molecular diagnosis of PCD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic heterogeneity of PCD is high and the clinical diagnosis is difficult.
DNAH5 is the main cause of PCD and that the phenotypic variability of PCD is mainly due to the genetic heterogeneity of the disease.
PCD should be considered as a clinical diagnosis, not only as a genetic diagnosis.
